text:
R. c. Sidawi

2026 QCCM 5

MUNICIPAL COURT OF

THE CITY OF MONTREAL

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT
OF MONTREAL

No:

124-051-855

DATE: January 26, 2026

______________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE MARIE-JOSÉE DIONNE

______________________________________________________________________

HIS MAJESTY THE KING

PROSECUTION

v.

IBRAHIM SIDAWI

DEFENDANT

______________________________________________________________________

SENTENCING DECISION

______________________________________________________________________

BACKGROUND

[
1
]

On July 29, 2025, at the conclusion of his
trial, the defendant (hereinafter referred to as the offender) was found guilty
on one count of criminal harassment
[1]
. The event occurred on January 10, 2024.

[
2
]

The offender and the victim
do not know each other.
On the day
of the event, the victim's vehicle was equipped with an Israeli flag.

[
3
]

It is in this context that
the offender's and the victim's vehicles crossed each other on the road. The offender,
whose grandfather is a native of Palestine, felt provoked by the display of the
flag considering the ongoing conflict between Israel and Palestine. The offender
first tried to obstruct the victim’s path, waved his finger from right to left
to say "No" in disapproval, and then gave her the finger and said,
"Fuck Israel." After the victim managed to get around his car, the
offender continued to follow her.
At some point, the offender stopped his car beside her, holding his
phone in her direction to photograph her.

[
4
]

The victim was so afraid that she called her
husband and 911 and she decided not to go pick-up her children. But then the
offender left the premises and turned right while the victim was going
straight. As she thought he had stopped following her, she finally went to the
school.

[
5
]

Once arrived, she saw the offender's car parked
on the street. Due to various incidents in the previous two years since the
beginning of the conflict between Israel and Palestine, a security guard was
stationed in front of the Jewish school to which a synagogue is annexed. She
informed him of the situation by pointing to the offender's vehicle. As the
security guard approached him, the offender left the scene.

[
6
]

The offender has no criminal record.

POSITION OF PARTIES

[
7
]

The defense requests a conditional discharge.

[
8
]

Pertaining the best interests criteria, she
argues the incident was isolated and not premeditated, noting the offender's
emotional state tied to his Palestinian background. She states the guilty
verdict has made it clear that such behavior is unacceptable.

[
9
]

She invokes two risks of prejudice: one in terms
of immigration, the other in terms of employment. The offender, a 30-year-old man
who recently married and moved to Florida, cannot leave the U.S. without
harming his citizenship prospects, as confirmed by immigration lawyer letters
dated October 3 and November 4, 2025. A criminal record would also negatively
impact his application, so a conditional discharge could alleviate these
consequences. Professionally, he holds a computer science degree from Montreal
and has experience in software engineering but is currently unemployed due to
work restrictions. A letter from
Good Times LLC
indicates future job
opportunities depend on a clean criminal record.

[
10
]

With respect to the public interests, she
invokes the effects of the conviction and the nature of the offence, which
already have consequences for the proceedings related to the offender's
citizenship application. This, combined with a donation of 200$, she argues
that the objectives of general denunciation and deterrence are met.

[
11
]

The prosecution is asking for a suspended
sentence with a probation of two years with conditions to protect the victim.
She points out, as an aggravating factor, the fact that this is a hate crime.
While she recognizes that the best interests of the offender have been
established, in her view, the discharge does not meet the objectives of
denunciation and deterrence and would be contrary to the public interest.

[
12
]

The defense agrees with the probation period and
the conditions.

QUESTION

[
13
]

Like the parties, the Court concludes that the best
interests have been demonstrated. Rather, the issue is whether granting a
conditional discharge would be contrary to the public interest.

THE LAW

[
14
]

Sections 718 et seq. of the
Criminal Code

set
out the principles and factors that the Court must consider in sentencing.

[
15
]

The purpose of sentencing is to denounce the
behaviour and harm caused to the victim and the community, to deter offenders
and others from committing offences, to isolate the offender from society, when
necessary, to promote reintegration into society, to ensure that harm is
remedied, and to create a sense of offender responsibility.

[
16
]

The Court must also apply the principle of
harmonization of sentences, and all this must be adapted to the offender's
personal situation.

[
17
]

The fundamental principle of this assessment, or
the keystone, remains the principle of proportionality, that is, that the
sentence must be proportionate to the act committed.

[
18
]

The sentencing exercise therefore requires
consideration of aggravating and mitigating factors, the objective and
subjective seriousness of the offence. The degree of culpability and
responsibility of the offender and the impact on the victim must be considered,
as well as the offender's personal circumstances and the collateral
consequences of the conviction. As establish by
R. v. Pham
,

2013
SCC 15
, the consequences of immigration are a factor that the Court must
consider in order to ensure that the imposition of the sentence does not have a
disproportionate impact on the offender.

[
19
]

Notwithstanding the above, the Supreme Court of Canada
in
Pham
also emphasized the importance of not distorting the nature of
the sentence by placing undue weight on its collateral consequences.

[
20
]

Section 730(1)
Cr.c.
provides that the
court may grant a discharge where the offence does not carry a minimum penalty
and is not punishable by 14 years’ imprisonment or life imprisonment, but only
if the following criteria are met: (1) the discharge is in the best interests
of the accused, and (2) it is not contrary to the public interest. The Court
notes at the outset that the offence of harassment is punishable by a maximum
sentence of 10 years in prison and carries no minimum sentence.

[
21
]

To satisfy the best interests test, the offender must establish a real possibility of prejudice and good
character.

[
22
]

With respect to the public interest test, the
Quebec Court of Appeal reiterated the principles as follows in
Ivanov v. R.,
2025 QCCA 301
, at paras.

78-80
:

[78] The
public interest is assessed in light of the need for general deterrence, the
objective and subjective seriousness of the offence and its impact on the
community. It is also worth noting that the granting of a discharge does
not have to
be
in the public interest, even if it must
not
going against it.

[79] With
respect to maintaining public confidence in the justice system, this factor
must be assessed in light of the opinion of a reasonable and well-informed
person about the functioning of the justice system, the offence context and the
offender's profile
.

[80]
Throughout this assessment process, the sentencing judge must not lose sight of
the possibility, if demonstrated, that an offender will one day become a person
of service to his or her community. Authors Parent and
Desrosiers write that "[t]he public interest is not to interfere with the
efforts already undertaken by the accused to ensure his reintegration into
society". [references omitted] [free translation]

[
23
]

The case law also recognizes that a discharge is
not an exceptional measure and that the objectives of deterrence and
denunciation can be achieved by imposing strict conditions as part of a
probation order.

ANALYSIS AND DECISION

[24]

EVIDENCE ON SENTENCE

[25]

Although the offender did not testify, his
lawyer filed various documents relating to

his employment situation and
his immigration status, which the Court will return to.

[26]

As for the victim, the prosecution filed the
Victim Impact Statement
[2]
.

The victim reports in great
detail the consequences she has suffered in various ways.

[27]

Emotionally, she experienced several months of
anxiety, fear and insecurity, suffering from insomnia, nightmares, flashbacks
and panic attacks. This anxiety has affected her family relationships and her
ability to care for her children. She felt a profound loss of security and
freedom for herself and her loved ones. She now avoids certain journeys,
remaining hypervigilant.

[28]

She expresses anger at being targeted because of
her Jewish identity and support for Israel. Her family was also affected, with
her husband sharing her worries and her children perceiving her anxiety. She
consults a psychologist to manage the trauma and her anxiety.

[29]

She questioned her sense of belonging to
Montreal and her freedom to express her identity, to the point of considering
leaving the country.

[30]

On a physical level, she suffered from various
psychosomatic symptoms (headaches, digestive disorders, muscle tension,
aggravation of an immune disorder).

[31]

Economically, she was unable to work for several
weeks, she suffered financial losses and professional disruption and also had
to bear indirect costs related to the legal proceedings.

[32]

MITIGATING AND AGGRAVATING FACTORS

[33]

In this case, the Court considers, as mitigating
factors, the fact that the offender has no criminal record and is an asset to
society.

[34]

Although the offender did not plead guilty, the
Court takes into account the fact that this lack of a plea could not be
considered an aggravating factor but rather deprived the offender of an
additional mitigating factor.

[35]

As an aggravating factor, the Court finds that
the offence was motivated by hate based on race, national or ethnic origin
[3]
.

[36]

OBJECTIVE AND SUBJECTIVE GRAVITY

[37]

The offence of harassment is punishable by 10 years’
imprisonment. The Ontario Court of Appeal held
[4]
in
R. v. Sabir
,
2018 ONCA 91
, para.46, that the offence of
criminal harassment generally requires courts to send a message to the accused
and the public that such conduct cannot be tolerated and must be deterred.

[38]

The objective gravity of the crime is high
because not only the victim was targeted because of the exercise of her right
to express solidarity with her community, but also because of the significant
consequences she suffered. The fact of being followed to her children's school
adds to her psychological consequences.

[39]

If it is an isolated event, the offender's
degree of responsibility is high. Indeed, the gratuitous nature of the crime,
its duration and the distance over which the event occurred demonstrate the
persistence of the offender in his actions despite the opportunity he had to stop
harassing the victim by pulling himself together once his turn to the right had
begun.

[40]

In light of all of the above, it is important to
determine first whether granting a discharge would be contrary to the public interest.

[41]

Since the offender’s best interests remains the first
criterion that require to be analysed for such a sentence, the Court concludes first
of all that this criterion is established, for the following reasons.

Offender's best interests

[42]

Risk of prejudice

[43]

A real risk of prejudice is established on two
fronts: at the professional level and at the immigration level.

[44]

At the professional level

[45]

The offender holds a bachelor in computer
science. He finished studying in Montreal. The defense filed proof of different
work experiences after his degree, heading in the track of software
engineering. As he is not allowed to work in the United States for now, he
currently does not have a job right now. The defense deposited a letter from
Good
Times LLC
dated from 29 July 2025 to establish a possible career as a
software engineer. However, a background check on his criminal record
[5]

must be made
because a criminal conviction or a pending legal matter would disqualify him.

[46]

The content of the letter from
Good Times LLC

demonstrates that the company has a protocol in place to ensure the security
and maintain the trust and integrity of its operations by refusing to hire a
candidate with a criminal record or a pending legal matter. The evidence shows
that in the absence of these elements, the company is seriously considering the
offender's application as a software engineer.

[47]

At the immigration level

[48]

According to the two letters from immigration
lawyer Sam Badawi, there are consequences related to both a guilty verdict and
a pending case. Referring to the relevant legislation, Me
Badawi says that a criminal record involving harassment
could jeopardize the approval of his pending application and even result in a
refusal of his citizenship application. It can also affect his ability to
establish the evidence of good character required to qualify for citizenship,
in addition to triggering an additional immigration test or proceeding. Also,
the single charge of criminal harassment, even without conviction, can
significantly harm the immigration process.

[49]

Good character

[50]

As already mentioned, the offender did not
testify at the sentencing hearing and therefore the Court has no evidence of
any remorse. However, since he is 30 years old and has no criminal record,
there is no basis to conclude that he is likely to reoffend or that he is not a
person of good character. Moreover, as the evidence at trial showed, the event
occurred in a circumscribed context, namely during a period of great stress
when he had just failed an exam and his grandfather was dying. There is no
evidence to suggest that he presents a specific deterrence and rehabilitation
problem.

[51]

In addition, there are the deterrent effects of
the judicial process recognized by case law in the case of first offenders.

[52]

For all these reasons, the Court finds that the
offender has established that it is in his best interests to be discharged.

[53]

QUESTION:

[54]

IS THE GRANTING OF A CONDITIONAL DISCHARGE
CONTRARY TO THE PUBLIC INTEREST?

[55]

The prosecution believes that granting a
discharge would be contrary to the public interest mainly because of the
objectives of general denunciation and deterrence.

[56]

The defense argues that these objectives have
been achieved because as there is already a guilty
verdict, this case will already be flagged by immigration customs in the US. So,
the offender will already have to explain himself about this case to work
inside his citizenship process for the next three years.

[57]

She pleads that the donation of $200 will allow
the offender to make amends for the wrongs. This may seem low, but this is
because the offender is unemployed and he's not able to
support his family for the moment. In fact, his parents
are supporting him right now.

[58]

She concludes by emphasizing the fact that the
victim may be reassured by the fact that, in accordance with the consequences
of the guilty finding and the immigration case implications, the offender is
unable to return to Canada for a period of three years. She concludes that this,
therefore, also contributes to meeting the objectives of protecting the public
and preventing recidivism.

[59]

Upon reading the
Victim impact statement
,
the Court understood that in the eyes of the victim, the granting of a
discharge appeared like if the criminal charge was dropped, which she would
feel like a great injustice. According to her, it is as if people in Quebec and
Canada could get away without true consequences despite their hateful and
criminal behaviours. She states that she counts on the court to set a precedent
by providing the maximum consequences allowed by law for the offender, so that
others will understand that these hateful and terrorizing behaviors are not
acceptable in our city, our province and our country.

[60]

The Court noted from these remarks the extent of
the consequences suffered on the victim, particularly on the emotional level,
and, with good reason, the great injustice suffered by the fact that she had
been targeted only because of her origins and despite her right to freedom of
speech.

[61]

It is true that in its analysis, the Court must
ensure to not undermine public confidence in the
judicial system, but it should be remembered that this factor must be assessed
in light of the opinion of a reasonable and well-informed person on the
functioning of the justice system, the offence context and the offender's
profile. Moreover, this objective must be considered in light of all other
sentencing objectives.

[62]

As the Honourable Justice Vauclair noted in
R.
c. Auclair,
2006 QCCQ 7093
, at para.

24-25
,
the objectives of denunciation and
deterrence are not satisfied only by the imposition of a criminal conviction.

[63]

Further, as he stated in

Harbour c. R.,
2017 QCCA 204
, at para.93
, s
entencing
must not become a response to crime alone rather than a sentence that is just
and proportionate to the crime and the offender. Also, in the context of this
decision, he points out, at paragraph 95,
that a sentence of discharge has been upheld on appeal even
in situations that normally engage the objective of general deterrence and
denunciation,

[64]

In addition, he reminds us, just like in the
case of a suspended sentence, that a discharge can be revoked in the event of a
criminal conviction, even for a breach of probation

referring to
section 730(4)
Cr.c.
Thus, the judge may set
aside the discharge and impose a sentence on the offender for the original
offence in addition to any other penalty. This is
without forgetting that such an order will protect the public.

[65]

As noted in
R.
v
. Meneses,
(1976),

1974 CanLII 1659 (ON CA)
, 25 C.C.C. (2d) 115 (O.C.A.):

12 It is
always to be borne in mind that a person who is granted a conditional discharge
does not go scot-free after committing the offence. In this case the accused is
subject to the terms of the probation order, and in the event that the terms of
the probation order are met, she will have earned her discharge. If the terms
are not met she may be brought back and sentenced for the offence, and a
conviction will be recorded against her
[6]
.

[66]

Thus, care must be taken to ensure that the
objectives of denunciation and deterrence do not lead to a disproportionate
sentence
[7]

and to strike an appropriate balance between the interests of society and the
offender.

[67]

It is therefore incorrect to conclude that the
granting of a discharge in this case would lead in the same result as if the
offender had been acquitted or the charge withdrawn and would have escaped
without any consequences.

[68]

On the contrary, the evidence shows that the
offender is already suffering significant consequences by reason of the guilty
verdict alone, as it delays and complicates his immigration process, even
risking compromising his citizenship application. Moreover, for this reason and
as the sentence is pending, he cannot return to work despite his academic
qualifications and employment experience.

[69]

The Court considers that, in the context of the 30-year-old
offender's first experience in court, together with the fact that he still has
to overcome the obstacles described as a result of this situation, this is
sufficient, in addition to the donation and the conditions with which he will
have to comply for two years,  to denounce hateful acts and send the message
that even in the case of an isolated act, it is not tolerated.

[70]

The offender is very lucky to have the financial
support of his relatives. The fact remains that without his actions, he would
not have had to depend on others despite his academic and professional
background. In this regard, it illustrates the importance of being an active
citizen in society.

[71]

For the next two years, he will have to ensure
that he does not contravene the conditions imposed, without the Court being
able to impose a sentence resulting in a criminal conviction that could destroy
his immigration efforts, but also both professionals and personals. These
consequences cannot be minimized nor be compared to a withdrawal of the charge.

[72]

During the duration of the probation order, the
victim will benefit from double protection for her safety, namely that imposed
by this Court, but also that resulting from the offender’s poor immigration
posture that preventing him, namely, from leaving the United States without
risking compromising everything.

[73]

In order to emphasize denunciation and deterrence, and despite the
offender's limited financial resources, the Court imposed an obligation on him
to make a donation of $2000 rather than $200. This takes into account the
letter from
Good Times LLC
which states that the offender is qualified
for the job if he has no criminal convictions or pending cases. The Court also
takes into account the scheduled appointment with immigration in October 2026,
which should change his situation.

[74]

This donation makes it possible to satisfy the principle of
reparation
for the harm caused and
to make the offender aware of
his responsibilities
. This makes it
possible to reconcile
the best
interests of the offender and the public interest:
Sadak v. R.,
2021
QCCA 1938
.
By
granting a discharge, the Court finds that the offender's employment
prospects are high and that he can reasonably afford the costs of a donation
that is higher than the proposed one in an appropriate period of time.

[75]

In light of all of the above, the Court finds
that the imposition of a criminal conviction would be disproportionate and that
a reasonable and informed person would consider the granting of a conditional
discharge to be reasonable in the circumstances.

[76]

The Court concludes that the granting of a
conditional discharge is not contrary to the public interest.

FOR THESE REASONS,

THE COURT:

[77]

GRANTS
a
conditional discharge with a probation order of two years and subject to the
following conditions:

[78]

- Keep the peace and have good behavior;

[79]

- Remain at the address where he currently
resides;

[80]

- Notify the Court of any change of address or
name and notify immediately of any   change in employment or occupation;

[81]

- Respond to all summonses from the Court;

[82]

-  Within eighteen months, pay the sum of $2000
to the Registry of the Court, which sum must be forwarded by the Registry to
the
Crime Victims Assistance Center
(CAVAC);

[83]

- Refrain from communicating with A…B… and her
children, directly or indirectly;

[84]

- Not be within a radius of 250 meters from A…B…'s
and her children’s home, school or place of work;

[85]

- Not be within a radius of 50 meters from A…B...
and her children;

[86]

- Not possessing weapons or imitation weapons.

[87]

ORDERS
the
offender to pay the surcharge;

[88]

ALL WITH FEES
,
AND THIS, WITHIN EIGHTEEN MONTHS.

MARIE-JOSÉE DIONNE,
Q.J.M.C
.
